summary: Akong Tulku Rinpoche (1939–2013) worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He founded the Kagyu Samye Ling Monastery and Tibetan Centre in 1967 and served as its abbot (attested 2009).

Akshara Ravishankar Parmeswaran is a scholar in Indology and philosophy. A doctoral candidate at the University of Chicago (attested 2026), Parmeswaran is attested as a researcher at Ghent University in 2026.
Akshay Ramanlal Desai (1915–1994) worked in history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Mumbai from circa 1935 to 1946, working under Govind Sadashiv Ghurye from circa 1940 to 1946.

Alan Avdagić specializes in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied as a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter at the Free University of Berlin (attested 2026) and held a post at the University of Würzburg.

Alan Entwistle (1949–1996) was an Indology and religious studies scholar who taught Heidi R. M. Pauwels. He studied at the University of Southampton (circa 1967–1970) and SOAS University of London (circa 1970–1978).

Alan Fox specializes in philosophy, sinology, and religious studies. After earning his PhD at Temple University (attested 1988), he served at the University of Delaware as a professor in 1992 and as associate professor of philosophy (attested 2013–2014).

Alan Gerard Wagner is a scholar of Buddhist studies and sinology. He earned his PhD at Harvard University (attested 2008) under Parimal G. Patil, also studying under Robert M. Gimello, Charles Hallisey, Carl Bielefeldt, and Masatoshi Nagatomi.
Alan Gowans (1923–2001) was a scholar in history and archaeology who taught Michael Willis. He studied at the University of Toronto (1946) and Princeton University (1948, 1950).

Alan John Bayard Wace (1879–1957) was a historian and archaeologist. He studied at Pembroke College under Robert Alexander Neil, and held posts at the British School at Athens, Victoria and Albert Museum, University of Cambridge, and Alexandria University.

Alan Lomax (1915–2002) studied at Choate Rosemary Hall, St. Mark's School of Texas, Harvard University (~1932–1933), the University of Texas at Austin (~1934–1936), and Columbia University (~1939–1940).
Alan Nussbaum (born 1947) is a linguist and Indologist. He completed his studies at Harvard University circa 1969–1976 and held a faculty post at Cornell University from circa 1985 to 2021.

Alan Sponberg (1944–2017) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and sinology who earned his Ph.D. from the University of British Columbia. He served as a professor at Princeton (attested 1980–1987) and taught at Stanford (attested 1988).

Alan Watts (1915–1973) was a religious studies, philosophy, and Buddhist studies scholar educated at Bexley Seabury Seminary. He held positions at Northwestern University, the American Academy of Asian Studies, Harvard University, San Jose State University, and the Esalen Institute.

Alasdair MacIntyre (1929–2025) was a philosopher educated at Queen Mary University and the University of Manchester. He held appointments at the University of Essex, Brandeis University, the University of Notre Dame, Duke University, and London Metropolitan University.

Alasdair Urquhart (born 1945) is a philosopher who studied at the University of Edinburgh and the University of Pittsburgh. He taught at the University of Toronto Mississauga (1973–1975) and became an emeritus professor at the University of Toronto (1986).

Alastair Gornall is a scholar in Buddhist studies, Indology, and linguistics who earned his PhD from Cambridge (circa 2008–2013). He held posts at SOAS (circa 2014–2016), the Singapore University of Technology and Design, and the Pali Text Society.

Albert Debrunner (1884–1958) was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Jacob Wackernagel and Ferdinand Sommer. He held professorial posts at Zurich, Greifswald, Bern, and Jena, and taught linguistics at the University of Basel.

Albert Grünwedel (1856–1935) was an Indologist, Tibetologist, and archaeologist who earned his doctorate at the University of Munich. He spent decades at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, serving as director from 1904 to 1921, and held an honorary professorship at Berlin.

Albert Hoefer (1812–1883) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Greifswald, Göttingen, and Berlin. He spent his academic career at the University of Greifswald from circa 1840 to 1883, serving as extraordinary professor from 1847 to 1880.
Albert Hofmann (1906–2008) studied at the University of Zurich from circa 1925 to 1929. He subsequently held a post at Novartis from circa 1929 to 1971.
